messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Arjun

Arjun was twenty-three when he was stopped by police outside a convenience store in Queens. He had ducked in for milk on a Friday evening, and when he came out, an officer called him over. There was a report of a robbery two blocks away, the officer said—a man matching his description. Arjun, whose family had lived in America for fifteen years and who had never been in trouble, explained this calmly. He was cooperative. He stood still as the officer patted him down, his hands moving across Arjun's chest and ribs and legs with a methodical pressure. It was cold that night, unseasonably so for October, and Arjun remembers the officer's hands as cold too—the shock of them through his thin shirt, the grip firm and impersonal. A second officer arrived. They told him to turn around. They told him to put his hands behind his back. He did. The cuffs were metal and tight, and they took him to the precinct, where he sat in a holding cell for eight hours before his mother came, before someone checked the store camera and saw that he had been inside the store when the robbery happened three blocks away.

The case was dropped. But something in Arjun had fractured.

In the months that followed, he returned to his job as an editor at a small publishing house in Manhattan, and he tried to move forward. He married Priya, a woman his parents had introduced him to, and they found an apartment in Forest Hills. But the world had become a place of hidden threats. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt absolute, that he was incapable of handling what life demanded of him. When he thought about that evening—about the pressure of the officer's hands, the cold seeping through his clothes, the smell of the precinct's fluorescent-lit holding cell, a chemical tang he could not quite name—grief would flood through him so completely that he could barely breathe. His body would remember the position he had held in those cuffs, his hands locked behind him, and he would feel his shoulders draw back and his spine curve inward, as if the memory were not something he was recalling but something happening to him again.

The triggers came without warning. A cold hand on his shoulder—Priya touching him on a winter morning—sent him spiraling. Being alone with Priya in their bedroom became impossible. He would find reasons to leave the room, to stay late at the office, to sleep on the couch. He could not explain to her why her presence, her closeness, felt dangerous, felt like it was pulling him toward something he could not survive. When she tried to talk to him about it, when she sat beside him on the bed and asked what was wrong, he felt the edges of reality beginning to dissolve. He would feel unreal, as if he were watching himself from outside his body, and the panic that followed was worse than any physical sensation.

At work, his ability to focus had deteriorated. He would be reviewing a manuscript and suddenly smell the precinct again—that chemical, metallic odor—and lose twenty minutes to the memory. His supervisor had begun to notice. Last month, he had missed a deadline for the first time in four years. His supervisor, a woman, had called him into her office to discuss it. Sitting across from her, he had felt the dissociation creeping in at the edges of his vision, and he had made an excuse and left. He had not been back to the office since.

It was Priya who finally insisted he see someone. She was crying when she said it, frustrated and frightened in equal measure. She told him that nothing he did seemed to help, that he was pulling away from her, that he seemed to believe nothing good could ever happen to him again. She was right. Arjun knew she was right, and knowing it only deepened his conviction that he was broken, that he had failed at the most basic task of being a functional human being. He was terrified of what a therapist might tell him, but he was more terrified of losing Priya, of confirming that he truly was incapable of holding onto anything that mattered.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: Patient is 26, but vignette states Arjun was 23 when the incident occurred: The vignette does not establish Arjun's current age. While it states he was 23 at the time of the police stop, there is no indication of how much time has passed since then or what his present age is. The patient's stated age is 26, which would suggest approximately 3 years have elapsed, but this is not made explicit in the narrative. For demographic validation, the approximate current age should be contextually clear.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Arjun was twenty-three when he was stopped by police outside a convenience store in Queens. He had ducked in for milk on a Friday evening, and when he came out, an officer called him over. There was a report of a robbery two blocks away, the officer said—a man matching his description. Arjun, whose family had lived in America for fifteen years and who had never been in trouble, explained this calmly. He was cooperative. He stood still as the officer patted him down, his hands moving across Arjun's chest and ribs and legs with a methodical pressure. It was cold that night, unseasonably so for October, and Arjun remembers the officer's hands as cold too—the shock of them through his thin shirt, the grip firm and impersonal. A second officer arrived. They told him to turn around. They told him to put his hands behind his back. He did. The cuffs were metal and tight, and they took him to the precinct, where he sat in a holding cell for eight hours before his mother came, before someone checked the store camera and saw that he had been inside the store when the robbery happened three blocks away. The case was dropped. But something in Arjun had fractured.

Three years had passed since that October evening, and Arjun was now twenty-six, though the years in between felt both compressed and infinite. In the months immediately following his release, he had returned to his job as an editor at a small publishing house in Manhattan, and he had tried to move forward. He married Priya, a woman his parents had introduced him to, and they found an apartment in Forest Hills. On the surface, his life had the shape it was supposed to have. But the world had become a place of hidden threats. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt absolute, that he was incapable of handling what life demanded of him—that something fundamental in his capacity to function had been damaged in those eight hours, and that no amount of time would repair it. When he thought about that evening—about the pressure of the officer's hands, the cold seeping through his clothes, the smell of the precinct's fluorescent-lit holding cell, a chemical tang he could not quite name—grief would flood through him so completely that he could barely breathe. His body would remember the position he had held in those cuffs, his hands locked behind him, and he would feel his shoulders draw back and his spine curve inward, as if the memory were not something he was recalling but something happening to him again.

The triggers came without warning and with a specificity that made no logical sense to him. A cold hand on his shoulder—Priya touching him on a winter morning—sent him spiraling into a panic so acute that his vision would narrow and his heart would hammer against his ribs. Being alone with Priya in their bedroom became impossible. He would find reasons to leave the room, to stay late at the office, to sleep on the couch. He could not explain to her why her presence, her closeness, felt dangerous, felt like it was pulling him toward something he could not survive. When she tried to talk to him about it, when she sat beside him on the bed and asked what was wrong, he felt the edges of reality beginning to dissolve. He would feel unreal, as if he were watching himself from outside his body, hovering above the scene like a ghost observing a stranger's marriage collapse, and the panic that followed was worse than any physical sensation. The dissociation frightened him more than the panic itself—it meant he was losing his grip on what was real.

At work, his ability to focus had deteriorated to the point where it was no longer sustainable. He would be reviewing a manuscript and suddenly smell the precinct again—that chemical, metallic odor—and lose twenty minutes to the memory, his hands gripping the desk as if he might fall through it. His supervisor had begun to notice. Last month, he had missed a deadline for the first time in four years. His supervisor, a woman, had called him into her office to discuss it. Sitting across from her, he had felt the dissociation creeping in at the edges of his vision, and he had made an excuse and left. He had not been back to the office since. The publishing house had sent two emails asking about his status. He had not responded to either.

It was Priya who finally insisted he see someone. She was crying when she said it, frustrated and frightened in equal measure. She told him that nothing he did seemed to help, that he was pulling away from her, that he seemed to believe nothing good could ever happen to him again. She was right. Arjun knew she was right, and knowing it only deepened his conviction that he was broken, that he had failed at the most basic task of being a functional human being. He was terrified of what a therapist might tell him, terrified that speaking the memories aloud would make them more real, more permanent. But he was more terrified of losing Priya, of confirming that he truly was incapable of holding onto anything that mattered. He had made the appointment on a Tuesday morning, sitting alone in their apartment while Priya was at work, and now he was sitting in a waiting room wondering if admitting he needed help was itself another failure, or if it might somehow be the first thing he had done right since the moment those cuffs had closed around his wrists.
